newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-LEWIS DESERVES HIS LESS THAN STAR STATUS, TRAINER SAYS.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-LEWIS DESERVES HIS LESS THAN STAR STATUS, TRAINER SAYS.

text.p: Usually a fighter's cornermen will rant loud and long about the respect their fighter should be getting, but Lennox Lewis's trainer thinks his man deserves his less than awesome image.

It's not because Emanuel Steward doesn't think Lewis is talented, it's because the World Boxing Council (WBC) champion has not had the kind of fights that win the hearts and minds of the boxing public.
Lewis's relatively low rating in the opinion polls is "fair what he's getting right now," Steward says. "Unfortunately he has not been in super-impressive fights."
In the upcoming July 12 defence of his title in Lake Tahoe, Nevada, the 31-year-old Lewis "needs to really finish" fellow-Briton Henry Akinwande, said Steward.
Akinwande, 31, has a 32-0-1 record and relinquished his lighty-regarded World Boxing Organisation (WBO) crown to fight Lewis.

In a telephone conference call from Big Bear, California, where Lewis is training for his scheduled 12-round fight with Akinwande, Steward reminded a reporter that Lewis should have received more respect for his grueling fight last May against a very tough Ray Mercer.
He was correct but, of course, one fight does not make a career, and certainly not a warrior.

The Mercer fight was one of the few times the often tentative Lewis, who usually will not risk getting a hangnail until his opponent is in serious trouble, traded punches and pain. Lewis eeked out a controversial majority decision after 10 rounds.
But Lewis is perhaps best remembered as the opponent of Oliver McCall when McCall dissolved psychologically in Las Vegas in February.

McCall, who stopped Lewis in 1994 to win the WBC title, had been in a drug rehabilitation programme right up to the day of the fight -- a fact the Nevada State Athletic Commission and everyone else associated with the fight well knew -- and seemed to suffer a mental breakdown on live television.
The tough-chinned McCall, who had never been knocked off his feet, broke down and cried in the ring and simply stopped fighting in his bid to regain the vacant WBC title.
The referee finally ended the fight in the fifth round after McCall kept walking away from Lewis.
Despite McCall's lack of offence, the taller and heavier Lewis could not knock McCall down.

Frank Maloney, Lewis's manager, a generally affable man, but not particularly brimming with sensitivity, especially for other fighters, said in reference to the McCall fight: "Who could look good against a lunatic? If he could have gotten to McCall he would have destroyed him."

Maloney, patched into the conference from London, said the Lewis-Akinwande fight originally was going to be on pay-per-view television in Britain but it was switched to regular cable as a way of "showcasing Lennox Lewis."

But then apparently realising that was admission of Lewis's less than super-star status, Maloney said, "no, not showcased. It was really Lennox who asked to switch so he could give something back to the fans."
The 6-foot-5 (1.95 m) Lewis said he was looking forward to matching up against Akinwande, another strapping heavyweight.
"I actually enjoy boxing a guy who I can see eye to eye with," said Lewis. "Akinwande's got some long arms and he's nice and tall and I can reach his chin real easy."
